2.title: Altered Mental Status
2.caseSummary: Elderly alcoholic patient with fall → subdural hematoma. Subdurals result from venous bleeding after blunt head trauma — bridging veins rupture. Risks: advanced age, alcoholism, anticoagulation. CT without contrast → neurosurgery for evacuation.
2.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is an elderly patient with a history of chronic alcoholism who presents to the emergency department with altered mental status following a recent fall. The patient has had episodic confusion and fluctuating consciousness since the fall. The subdural hematoma risk is elevated due to advanced age and chronic alcohol use, both of which contribute to brain atrophy and increased tension on bridging veins. Time is critical — expanding hematoma may cause mass effect and progressive neurological deterioration.

3.title: Pelvic Pain
3.chiefComplaint: Severe pelvic pain, worse with intercourse
3.caseSummary: Right adnexal mass in reproductive-age woman with severe pelvic pain and dyspareunia. Imaging (US/CT/MRI) → endometrioma. Treatment: laparotomy/laparoscopy by OB/GYN. Preventive counseling for smoking cessation and drug use.
3.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a reproductive-age woman who presents with severe pelvic pain that worsens with sexual activity. The pain is localized to the right adnexal region. Differential for a right adnexal mass in a reproductive-age female is broad and includes ectopic pregnancy, tuboovarian abscess, inflammatory bowel disease, ovarian mass, endometrioma, theca lutein cysts, and germ cell neoplasms. Imaging and appropriate surgical consultation are required.

4.title: Abdominal Pain
4.chiefComplaint: Abdominal pain, vomiting, lethargy x 2 days
4.caseSummary: New-onset Type 1 Diabetes presenting as DKA. Glucose in 600s. Treatment: IV fluids + insulin + K replacement. Monitor anion gap for resolution. Admit to ICU. Preventive: diabetes education, pap smear, HPV/Tdap vaccines, drug counseling.
4.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a 22-year-old woman with no known past medical history who presents to the emergency department with diffuse abdominal pain, lethargy, and vomiting for two days. The clinical picture is consistent with new-onset diabetic ketoacidosis — the abdominal pain is a common presenting feature of DKA, not a primary surgical abdomen.

5.title: Headache
5.caseSummary: Difficult diagnostic case — West Nile encephalitis. Fever + ataxia + maculopapular rash. CT/MRI to rule out stroke/mass → LP with CSF analysis (lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, elevated protein = viral) → WNV antibody confirms. Little treatment — supportive care. Preventive health: Pap, mammogram, Tdap.
5.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a 55-year-old woman who presents with fever, headache, and progressive ataxia. She has developed pink macular lesions on the left thigh. Neurological examination reveals cerebellar signs. The combination of fever, neurological symptoms, and characteristic rash in the appropriate season raises concern for arboviral encephalitis. West Nile virus is the leading consideration among mosquito-borne neuroinvasive diseases. Diagnostic workup must include brain imaging to rule out stroke or mass lesion, followed by lumbar puncture for CSF analysis.

6.title: Rash and Lethargy
6.caseSummary: Classic pediatric mononucleosis. Fever + pharyngitis + lymphadenopathy + splenomegaly. Monospot/EBV serology confirms. Symptomatic treatment: acetaminophen, rest. Avoid aspirin (Reye's) and amoxicillin/ampicillin (drug rash). Office management.
6.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a 6-year-old child who presents with fever, sore throat, malaise, and generalized rash. Exam reveals posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, palatal petechiae, and splenomegaly. The combination of pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, fever, and the characteristic maculopapular rash is classic for infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein-Barr virus. The differential includes other viral infections (CMV, acute HIV), streptococcal pharyngitis, and toxoplasmosis. Key management considerations: avoid amoxicillin/ampicillin (causes characteristic EBV rash), avoid aspirin (Reye syndrome risk in febrile children), and in older patients, restrict contact sports to prevent splenic rupture.

8.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a 19-year-old sexually active man who presents with dysuria, fevers, and chills. Rectal exam reveals an edematous, tender prostate — the key finding that localizes the infection to the prostate rather than the bladder or urethra alone. 11.caseSummary: Hepatitis A from cruise ship (fecal-oral) with aspiration pneumonia from vomiting. LFTs 2000-3000. Supportive care + CAP antibiotics + O2. Avoid acetaminophen. Inpatient admission.
11.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a man who recently returned from a cruise ship and presents with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, jaundice, and shortness of breath. He has RUQ tenderness on exam. LFTs are markedly elevated in the 2000-3000 range. The cruise ship travel and profoundly elevated transaminases are highly suspicious for acute viral hepatitis A (fecal-oral transmission). His episodes of vomiting led to aspiration pneumonia. Acetaminophen level should be checked to rule out overdose as a cause of acute liver injury. Management is supportive: IV fluids, antiemetics, oxygen for hypoxia, and antibiotics for aspiration pneumonia per ATS/IDSA guidelines (treat as community-acquired pneumonia; no anaerobic coverage needed without abscess/empyema). Acetaminophen is contraindicated with hepatic injury. Admit to inpatient unit.

12.title: Burning During Urination
12.chiefComplaint: Dysuria, purulent urethral discharge, scrotal swelling
12.caseSummary: Chlamydia urethritis — most common bacterial STI. NAAT on urine confirms. Azithromycin 1g PO once. Partner treated. Full STI panel. Office management.
12.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a sexually active young adult who presents with dysuria, purulent urethral discharge, and scrotal swelling. The patient admits to illicit drug use and risky sexual practices. Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common bacterial STI — an obligate intracellular pathogen. Co-infection with gonorrhea is common (40% of women, 20% of men), so empiric treatment for both is recommended even if only chlamydia is confirmed. Most cases are asymptomatic (80% women, 50% men), making the presence of overt urethritis clinically useful. First-line diagnosis is NAAT (DNA probe) on first-catch urine. Treatment: azithromycin 1g PO single dose OR doxycycline 100mg PO BID x 7 days. Sexual partners must be treated. Screen for all STIs (gonorrhea, HIV, hepatitis B/C, syphilis, HSV).

13.title: Abdominal Pain
13.caseSummary: NSAID-induced acute gastritis from chronic ibuprofen use for OA. Conservative management: stop NSAIDs, start PPI, switch to acetaminophen/topical diclofenac. Avoid EGD unless fails 2-4 weeks of conservative therapy. Office management.
13.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is an older man with chronic osteoarthritis who presents with epigastric abdominal pain of one week's duration. History reveals extensive, prolonged use of oral ibuprofen for knee pain. NSAIDs block both COX-1 and COX-2, impairing gastric prostaglandin production and disrupting mucosal defense — this is classic NSAID-induced gastropathy. Symptoms began one week ago and the patient is medically stable. Conservative management is key: discontinue NSAIDs, start a proton-pump inhibitor, and follow up in 2-4 weeks. If no improvement with conservative therapy, then EGD would be indicated, but ordering it now loses points — the USMLE tests restraint from invasive testing. H. pylori should be ruled out. For his osteoarthritis, switch to acetaminophen and/or topical diclofenac gel rather than oral NSAIDs. Address modifiable risk factors: smoking cessation and alcohol avoidance.

14.title: Facial and Upper Extremity Edema
14.chiefComplaint: Facial/upper extremity edema, severe hypertension, headache, blurry vision at 33 weeks
14.caseSummary: Pre-eclampsia with severe features at 33 weeks. BP 189/99 + headache + blurry vision. MgSO4 + IV labetalol + betamethasone + cesarean delivery by OB/GYN. Admit to ICU.
14.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a pregnant woman at 33 weeks gestation who presents with facial and upper extremity edema, severe hypertension (189/99), new-onset headaches, and blurry vision — signs of end-organ damage. Pre-eclampsia is defined as SBP > 140 or DBP > 90 developing after 20 weeks gestation WITH end-organ dysfunction (proteinuria, visual/cerebral disturbances, pulmonary edema, creatinine > 1.1, elevated LFTs, or thrombocytopenia < 100,000). With SBP > 160, she meets criteria for pre-eclampsia with severe features. Management triad: (1) Magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis to prevent progression to eclampsia, (2) IV labetalol or hydralazine for blood pressure control (labetalol is superior with fewer side effects), (3) Betamethasone for fetal lung maturity if delivering < 34 weeks. Definitive treatment is delivery — with severe features, deliver at ≥ 34 weeks. OB/GYN consult for cesarean section. Admit to ICU or inpatient unit — this is an emergency.

15.title: Chest Pain
15.chiefComplaint: Pleuritic chest pain, relieved by leaning forward
15.caseSummary: Idiopathic acute pericarditis. Pleuritic chest pain + diffuse ST elevation + small effusion on echo. NSAIDs + colchicine + PPI. Avoid pericardiocentesis and TEE. ER then outpatient management with rest.
15.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a man with no significant past medical history who presents with acute chest pain that is pleuritic (worse with inspiration) and positional (relieved by leaning forward). He has no history of recent viral infection, making this likely idiopathic pericarditis. ECG shows diffuse ST elevation. Echocardiogram reveals a small pericardial effusion — no tamponade physiology. Troponin is negative, ruling out MI. First-line treatment: NSAIDs (ibuprofen/naproxen) PLUS colchicine — colchicine reduces symptoms and decreases rate of recurrent pericarditis. Add a PPI/H2 blocker for GI protection with high-dose NSAID therapy. Rest until symptoms resolve — activity can trigger recurrence. Pericardiocentesis is NOT indicated for small, asymptomatic effusions (only for moderate/large effusions > 2 cm or tamponade). Transesophageal echo is unnecessary — transthoracic echo is sufficient.

17.title: Weight Loss and Night Sweats
17.chiefComplaint: Painless cervical lymphadenopathy, weight loss, night sweats
17.caseSummary: Classic Hodgkin's lymphoma: painless cervical lymphadenopathy + B-symptoms. Excisional biopsy → Reed-Sternberg cells (CD15+/CD30+). PET/CT for staging. ABVD chemotherapy. Office diagnosis → heme/onc referral.
17.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy and constitutional B-symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, fever). Hodgkin's lymphoma is a B-cell malignancy defined by Reed-Sternberg cells — 'owl-eyed' nucleoli with clear cytoplasm, CD15+ and CD30+. Excisional lymph node biopsy (NOT FNA) is required for diagnosis to preserve architecture for immunophenotyping and cytogenetics. CXR is initial screening. PET/CT for staging: Stage I (single node), II (≥2 nodes same side of diaphragm), III (both sides), IV (extranodal). Treatment: ABVD chemotherapy (Adriamycin, Bleomycin, Vinblastine, Dacarbazine) ± radiation for early stage. Check albumin as prognostic indicator. Screen for HIV and EBV, which can mimic lymphoma.

18.title: Constipation and Malaise
18.caseSummary: Colon adenocarcinoma. Constipation + malaise + positive FOBT. Colonoscopy with biopsy → CT staging → CEA → pre-op labs → NPO → colectomy. Office → surgery. 90% recurrences within 3 years — close follow-up essential.
18.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with constipation, malaise, nausea, and vomiting. Occult blood is positive. Colon cancer is the third most common cancer and third most common cause of cancer mortality in the US. Left colon masses present with obstructive symptoms (constipation, decreased stool caliber); right colon masses present with iron deficiency anemia from occult bleeding. Workup: colonoscopy with biopsy for diagnosis (NOT just flexible sigmoidoscopy — must examine entire colon). CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with contrast for staging (gold standard for metastasis screening). CEA level pre-op for prognosis and recurrence monitoring. Pre-op clearance: ECG, PT/PTT, type and screen, NPO. Treatment: surgical resection (colectomy) by colorectal surgery. If lymph node positive → adjuvant chemotherapy. Follow-up: CEA q3-6mo, CT annually x 5yr, colonoscopy at 1yr then q3yr.

19.title: Abdominal Pain
19.caseSummary: Complicated acute diverticulitis with 2 cm abscess. LLQ pain + fever + leukocytosis (SIRS). CT confirms. NPO + IV fluids + IV ceftriaxone/metronidazole. No drainage needed (<3-4 cm). Avoid colonoscopy. High-fiber diet at discharge.
19.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with the classic triad of diverticulitis: LLQ pain, low-grade fever, and leukocytosis. He has changes in bowel habits with nausea and vomiting. He meets SIRS criteria (fever >100.4°F, WBC >12,000). CT abdomen/pelvis with IV and oral contrast is the gold standard — findings include bowel wall thickening, pericolic fat stranding, and a 2 cm abscess (complicated diverticulitis). Abscesses <3-4 cm can be managed conservatively with antibiotics alone without percutaneous drainage. Colonoscopy and barium enema are CONTRAINDICATED in acute diverticulitis due to risk of perforation. Treatment: NPO for bowel rest, IV fluids, IV antibiotics (cefazolin + metronidazole, cefuroxime + metronidazole, ceftriaxone + metronidazole, or ampicillin/sulbactam). High-fiber diet at discharge for prevention.

20.title: Palpitations
20.caseSummary: Complete (3rd degree) AV block — likely fibrotic degeneration from aging + HTN. ECG: P and QRS dissociation. Troponin negative, TSH normal, chemistries normal, ESR normal — infectious/inflammatory unlikely. Temporary pacer → permanent pacemaker. ER → ICU/inpatient.
20.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is an older woman with hypertension on hydrochlorothiazide who presents with palpitations, syncope, dizziness, and hypotension. ECG demonstrates complete heart block (3rd degree AV block) — complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes with no relationship. This is a bradycardic rhythm. 21.title: Abdominal Pain
21.chiefComplaint: Alternating diarrhea/constipation, abdominal pain relieved by defecation
21.caseSummary: IBS diagnosis of exclusion in 29yo. Rome IV criteria met. Normal ESR/CRP, no alarm symptoms. Conservative management: diet + exercise + loperamide PRN. Avoid colonoscopy.
21.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a 29-year-old who presents with alternating diarrhea and constipation, abdominal pain relieved by defecation, and bloating — meeting Rome IV criteria for IBS (recurrent abdominal pain + ≥2 of: improvement with defecation, change in stool frequency, change in stool appearance). ESR and CRP are normal, ruling out inflammatory bowel disease. Stool studies are negative for infectious etiology. IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out celiac disease (anti-tTG, anti-endomysial antibodies), C. difficile, parasites, and colorectal cancer. Conservative management is key: high-fiber diet, lactose-free trial, exercise, trigger food avoidance. Loperamide PRN for diarrhea, antispasmodics (dicyclomine/hyoscyamine) PRN. Colonoscopy/sigmoidoscopy is NOT appropriate — invasive testing loses points in stable patients with normal screening labs. TCA/SSRI for refractory cases at follow-up.

22.title: Found Unconscious
22.chiefComplaint: Found unconscious, respiratory depression, suspected overdose
22.caseSummary: TCA overdose (suicide attempt). Obtunded + widened QRS + hypotension. Intubate → bicarb → charcoal → ICU. Psych consult after stabilization.
22.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a young woman found unconscious with respiratory depression, hypotension, and altered mental status. ECG shows widened QRS, prolonged QT — classic TCA cardiotoxicity. The 'Three C's' of TCA poisoning: Coma, Convulsions, Cardiac arrhythmias. Management priorities: ABCs — intubate for airway protection (GCS depressed), mechanical ventilation. IV fluids for hypotension (TCA blocks alpha-1 receptors → vasodilation). Sodium bicarbonate for cardiac toxicity (QRS >100ms or ventricular arrhythmia) — alkalinization to pH 7.45-7.55 favors non-ionized TCA, reducing sodium channel blockade. Activated charcoal via NG tube if within 2 hours of ingestion (airway must be secured first). 'Coma cocktail': check glucose, give thiamine before D50. Naloxone for possible opioid co-ingestion. CT head to rule out trauma (unwitnessed). Aspirin and acetaminophen levels for common co-ingestants. Psychiatry consult after stabilization for suicide attempt.

23.title: Shortness of Breath
23.chiefComplaint: Progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, LE edema
23.caseSummary: Systolic CHF exacerbation (NYHA III-IV). Prior MI + HTN. IV Lasix → NTG → continue lisinopril → add carvedilol before discharge. Admit to inpatient. Lifestyle: low Na, smoking cessation, vaccines.
23.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is an older man with history of prior myocardial infarction and hypertension on lisinopril who presents with progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, and bilateral lower extremity pitting edema. Exam reveals JVD, S3 gallop, pulmonary crackles, and expiratory wheezing. CXR shows pulmonary edema and cardiomegaly. Echo confirms reduced ejection fraction — systolic dysfunction. BNP is elevated. The most common cause of systolic HF is ischemic heart disease. NYHA Class III-IV (symptoms with minimal activity). Treatment: IV loop diuretic (furosemide) for volume overload, continue ACEI, add nitroglycerin for afterload reduction. Once acute exacerbation resolves and patient is euvolemic, start beta-blocker (carvedilol preferred per COMET trial — 17% survival benefit over metoprolol, though bisoprolol and metoprolol succinate also accepted). Digoxin for symptom control if needed. No stress tests until recovered. Admit to inpatient unit. Discharge: low-sodium diet, smoking cessation, alcohol avoidance, pneumococcal and zoster vaccines, Tdap.

28.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a sexually active young woman presenting with bilateral lower abdominal/pelvic pain, cervical motion tenderness, adnexal tenderness, purulent cervical discharge, fever, and leukocytosis. Pelvic inflammatory disease is an ascending infection from the lower genital tract — commonly Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae, though polymicrobial. Diagnosis is clinical based on CDC criteria: uterine/adnexal tenderness + cervical motion tenderness (minimum). Treatment: empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics covering chlamydia, gonorrhea, and anaerobes — ceftriaxone 250mg IM once + doxycycline 100mg PO BID x 14 days + metronidazole 500mg PO BID x 14 days. Partner treatment essential. Screen for other STIs. Admit if severe, TOA, pregnant, or failed outpatient treatment.

29.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a reproductive-age woman presenting with irregular, heavy vaginal bleeding without identifiable structural or systemic cause. This is dysfunctional uterine bleeding (DUB), most commonly anovulatory — unopposed estrogen stimulation leads to endometrial hyperplasia and irregular shedding. Diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out pregnancy, structural lesions (fibroids, polyps), thyroid dysfunction, coagulopathy, and malignancy. Workup: HCG (rule out pregnancy/complications), CBC (assess anemia from blood loss), TSH/prolactin, pelvic ultrasound (rule out structural causes), endometrial biopsy if age >45 or risk factors. Treatment depends on severity and fertility goals: hormonal regulation with combined OCPs or cyclic progestins. If acute heavy bleeding: high-dose estrogen or IV conjugated estrogens. Iron supplementation for anemia.

32.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute RUQ abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and fever. Pain may radiate to right shoulder or scapula. 33.title: Altered Mental Status
33.chiefComplaint: Gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, cognitive decline
33.caseSummary: NPH: classic triad + ventriculomegaly with normal LP opening pressure. High-volume LP shows gait improvement → VP shunt placed by neurosurgery. Reversible dementia — must recognize early.
33.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is an elderly patient presenting with the classic triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus: (1) gait disturbance ('magnetic gait' — feet feel stuck to floor), (2) urinary incontinence, and (3) progressive cognitive decline/dementia. NPH is one of the few reversible causes of dementia and must be recognized early. CT/MRI shows ventriculomegaly out of proportion to sulcal atrophy, without obstruction. LP opening pressure is NORMAL (<18 cm H2O) — this distinguishes NPH from obstructive hydrocephalus. High-volume LP (30-50 mL CSF removal) with pre- and post- gait assessment is diagnostic: improvement in gait after CSF removal supports the diagnosis and predicts response to VP shunting. Definitive treatment: ventriculoperitoneal shunt.

34.title: Headache
34.chiefComplaint: Severe headache, blurry vision, severely elevated BP
34.caseSummary: Hypertensive emergency with cerebral end-organ damage (headache + visual changes + papilledema). IV labetalol in ICU. Reduce MAP ≤25% in first hour. Avoid rapid normalization.
34.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with severe headache, blurred vision, and severely elevated blood pressure (>180/120). This is a hypertensive emergency — severe hypertension WITH evidence of acute end-organ damage (headache/visual changes suggesting cerebral involvement, possible papilledema, retinal hemorrhages). Must be distinguished from hypertensive urgency (severe HTN without end-organ damage — manage with oral meds as outpatient). Workup: fundoscopy (papilledema, hemorrhages, exudates), ECG (LVH, ischemia), CXR (pulmonary edema, aortic dissection signs), UA (proteinuria, hematuria), BMP (elevated Cr — renal damage), cardiac enzymes, CT head if focal neuro deficits. Treatment: IV antihypertensives in ICU — reduce MAP by no more than 25% in first hour (too rapid reduction causes cerebral/coronary hypoperfusion). Labetalol IV, nicardipine, or clevidipine. Goal: reduce DBP to 100-105 over 2-6 hours. Do NOT use short-acting nifedipine (risk of rapid uncontrollable hypotension).

35.title: Seizure
35.caseSummary: Delirium tremens: seizure + AMS + autonomic hyperactivity + hallucinations 24-72h after EtOH cessation. CIWA-guided benzodiazepines + thiamine + IVF + Mg/K. ICU admission.
35.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with new-onset seizure, altered mental status, autonomic hyperactivity (tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, hyperthermia), tremors, and visual/tactile hallucinations (formication). History reveals chronic heavy alcohol use with abrupt cessation 24-72 hours prior. This is alcohol withdrawal progressing to delirium tremens — a medical emergency with 5-15% mortality if untreated. Pathophysiology: chronic alcohol enhances GABA inhibition and suppresses NMDA glutamate excitation. Abrupt withdrawal → loss of GABA tone + rebound glutamate hyperactivity → CNS hyperexcitability. The CIWA-Ar score quantifies severity and guides treatment. Management: benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam, chlordiazepoxide) — symptom-triggered or fixed-schedule dosing until sedated but arousable. Thiamine before glucose (prevent Wernicke's). IV fluids for dehydration. Correct electrolytes (hypomagnesemia, hypokalemia common). Admit to ICU for severe DTs. Rule out other causes of seizure: CT head, EEG, tox screen, metabolic panel.

36.title: Headache
36.chiefComplaint: Severe headache, fever, stiff neck, photophobia, rash
36.caseSummary: Bacterial meningitis (meningococcal). Triad: headache + fever + nuchal rigidity + petechiae. CSF: neutrophilic pleocytosis, low glucose. Ceftriaxone + vanc + dexamethasone immediately. Droplet precautions. ICU.
36.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with severe headache, fever, photophobia, nuchal rigidity, and altered mental status. Exam reveals positive Kernig's sign (pain with knee extension when hip flexed 90°) and Brudzinski's sign (involuntary hip/knee flexion with passive neck flexion). Petechial/purpuric rash is present — meningococcemia causes DIC and purpura fulminans. This is a medical emergency. Do NOT delay antibiotics for CT or LP. Blood cultures + LP with CSF analysis (opening pressure, cell count with differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture). CSF: neutrophilic pleocytosis, low glucose (<40 or <2/3 serum), elevated protein, Gram-negative diplococci. Empiric antibiotics: ceftriaxone 2g IV + vancomycin + dexamethasone (before or with first dose). Add ampicillin if Listeria risk (age >50, immunocompromised). Droplet precautions for meningococcal. Chemoprophylaxis for close contacts (rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone).

38.chiefComplaint: Painless jaundice, weight loss, dark urine, clay-colored stools
38.caseSummary: Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma. Painless jaundice + Courvoisier's sign. CT pancreatic protocol + EUS-FNA → Whipple if resectable, palliative chemo/stent if not. Poor prognosis. Early palliative care.
38.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with painless jaundice, dark urine, clay-colored stools, pruritus, and weight loss — classic for malignant biliary obstruction. Courvoisier's sign: palpable, non-tender gallbladder in a jaundiced patient = malignancy until proven otherwise (most commonly pancreatic head adenocarcinoma). Pancreatic cancer most commonly arises in the head of the pancreas (70%), causing early obstructive jaundice. Late presentation is the rule — most are unresectable at diagnosis. Workup: CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast (pancreatic protocol — dual-phase) for staging. CA 19-9 tumor marker (not diagnostic but prognostic and monitors recurrence). ERCP/MRCP for biliary drainage if needed. Biopsy via EUS-FNA. If resectable (localized, no vascular involvement, no mets): pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure). If unresectable: palliative biliary stenting, chemotherapy (gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel or FOLFIRINOX). Poor prognosis — 5-year survival <10%.

41.title: Generalized Weakness
41.chiefComplaint: Generalized weakness, cola-colored urine, periorbital/ankle edema
41.caseSummary: PSGN in child. Cola urine + periorbital/ankle edema + HTN + AKI 1-4 weeks after strep pharyngitis. UA: RBC casts + proteinuria. Low C3. Supportive care: fluid restriction + furosemide. Excellent prognosis.
41.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a child who presents with generalized weakness, oliguria, cola-colored (dark brown) urine, periorbital and ankle edema (2+ pitting), and hypertension 1-4 weeks after a streptococcal pharyngitis or skin infection (impetigo). This is acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis — an immune complex-mediated (type III hypersensitivity) disease. Antigen-antibody complexes deposit in the glomerular basement membrane → complement activation → glomerular inflammation. Labs: UA shows hematuria (dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts — pathognomonic), proteinuria (<3.5g/day — nephritic, not nephrotic range). Low C3 complement (returns to normal in 6-8 weeks). Elevated ASO titer (pharyngitis) or anti-DNase B (skin infection). BMP shows elevated BUN/Cr (acute kidney injury). Diagnosis is clinical. Renal biopsy only if rapidly progressive GN or atypical course. Treatment: supportive — salt/fluid restriction, diuretics (furosemide) for hypertension and edema, antihypertensives if needed. Prognosis excellent in children (>95% complete recovery). Antibiotics if active strep infection. No immunosuppression needed.

42.title: Knee Pain
42.chiefComplaint: Acute severe knee pain, redness, swelling
42.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute onset severe monoarticular knee pain, erythema, warmth, and swelling. Pain began suddenly overnight — classic podagra (great toe) or knee involvement. History reveals dietary triggers (red meat, seafood, alcohol) or diuretic use. Gout is caused by monosodium urate crystal deposition in joints from chronic hyperuricemia. Definitive diagnosis: joint aspiration with synovial fluid analysis under polarized light microscopy — needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals. Do NOT give NSAIDs in renal impairment. First-line acute treatment: NSAIDs (indomethacin or naproxen), colchicine (within 36h of onset), or corticosteroids (oral prednisone or intra-articular injection). Colchicine: avoid in renal/hepatic impairment, CYP3A4 interactions. Long-term urate-lowering: allopurinol or febuxostat (start after acute flare resolves, with colchicine prophylaxis for 3-6 months). Target uric acid <6.0 mg/dL (or <5.0 for tophaceous gout).

43.title: Knee Pain
43.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute monoarticular knee pain, fever, and chills. The knee is warm, swollen, erythematous, and exquisitely tender with limited range of motion. Disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) is the most common cause of septic arthritis in sexually active young adults. Classic triad: tenosynovitis, dermatitis (pustular or vesiculopustular lesions), and migratory polyarthralgia progressing to monoarticular septic arthritis. Most commonly affects knee. Diagnosis: arthrocentesis with synovial fluid analysis (WBC >50,000, Gram stain may show Gram-negative diplococci, culture positive in only 50%). Also culture cervix, urethra, rectum, pharynx for N. gonorrhoeae. NAAT on synovial fluid. Treatment: ceftriaxone 1g IV daily initially, then switch to oral cefixime or fluoroquinolone based on sensitivities. If chlamydia co-infection possible (common), add doxycycline or azithromycin. Joint drainage (serial aspiration or arthroscopy). Partner treatment essential.

44.chiefComplaint: Chronic foul-smelling greasy diarrhea, bloating, weight loss
44.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with chronic foul-smelling, greasy diarrhea (steatorrhea), bloating, abdominal cramps, and weight loss. History reveals recent camping/hiking trip drinking untreated stream water. Giardia lamblia is a flagellated protozoan transmitted via fecal-oral route through contaminated water (common in hikers/campers — 'beaver fever'). Cysts are chlorine-resistant. Diagnosis: stool O&P (ova and parasites) — multiple samples needed (shedding intermittent). Stool Giardia antigen ELISA is more sensitive. String test (Entero-Test) if stool studies negative. Treatment: tinidazole (single dose) or metronidazole (5-7 days). Nitazoxanide for children. Paromomycin in pregnancy. Treat close contacts. Boil or filter water when camping.

45.title: Unresponsive
45.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is found unresponsive with pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression (RR <12), and decreased bowel sounds — the classic opioid toxidrome. 46.title: Weakness in Extremities
46.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with rapidly progressive symmetric ascending weakness beginning in the lower extremities, areflexia, and possible paresthesias. History often reveals antecedent infection (Campylobacter jejuni most common, also viral URI, EBV, CMV) or vaccination within 1-4 weeks. GBS is an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (AIDP) caused by molecular mimicry — antibodies against infectious agents cross-react with peripheral nerve antigens. Classic: ascending symmetric weakness + areflexia + albuminocytologic dissociation in CSF (elevated protein with normal WBC count). EMG/NCS shows demyelinating pattern. Critical complication: respiratory failure from diaphragm involvement — monitor FVC and NIF (negative inspiratory force). FVC <20 mL/kg or NIF <-30 cm H2O = elective intubation. Autonomic instability common (labile BP, arrhythmias). Treatment: IVIG (0.4g/kg/day x 5 days) or plasmapheresis — both equally effective. Do NOT give steroids (ineffective in GBS, unlike CIDP). ICU admission for monitoring. Prognosis: 85% recover, 3-5% mortality.

50.title: Headache
50.chiefComplaint: Severe unilateral orbital headache with lacrimation
50.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with severe unilateral orbital/supraorbital/temporal headache lasting 15-180 minutes, occurring in clusters (multiple times per day for weeks-months then remission). Associated ipsilateral autonomic features: lacrimation, conjunctival injection, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, eyelid edema, miosis/ptosis (Horner's). Patient is restless/agitated during attacks (unlike migraine where patient lies still). Triggers: alcohol during cluster period. More common in men. First-line acute treatment: high-flow 100% oxygen 12-15 L/min via non-rebreather (aborts attack within 15 min) AND/OR subcutaneous sumatriptan 6mg. Bridge therapy: verapamil (first-line prophylaxis), prednisone taper for rapid suppression. Avoid triggers during cluster period. Refer to neurology.

51.title: Altered Mental Status
51.chiefComplaint: Transient focal neurological deficit, resolves within hours
51.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with transient focal neurological deficit (unilateral weakness, aphasia, visual field defect) resolving completely within 24 hours (typically <1 hour). Aggressive risk factor management: statin, BP control, diabetes control, smoking cessation. Admit for expedited workup.

54.title: Yellow Baby
54.chiefComplaint: Jaundice in otherwise well-appearing term newborn
54.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a term newborn presenting with jaundice appearing after day 3-5 of life, clinically well-appearing, feeding well, gaining weight appropriately. Breastfeeding jaundice is the most common cause of prolonged neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Pathophysiology: inadequate breastfeeding intake → decreased stooling → increased enterohepatic circulation of bilirubin. Must distinguish from pathologic causes: hemolysis (ABO/Rh incompatibility, G6PD deficiency), sepsis, biliary atresia (conjugated), hypothyroidism. Key labs: total and direct bilirubin (unconjugated > conjugated by definition), CBC with reticulocyte count (anemia? hemolysis?), direct Coombs (immune hemolysis), G6PD screen. Plot on Bhutani nomogram for phototherapy threshold. Management: optimize breastfeeding (increase frequency, lactation consultation). Phototherapy if bilirubin exceeds threshold for gestational age and risk factors. Exchange transfusion if signs of bilirubin encephalopathy or failed phototherapy.

68.title: Muscle Weakness
68.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with progressive proximal muscle weakness, myalgias, and fatigue. History reveals concurrent use of simvastatin and gemfibrozil — a CONTRAINDICATED combination. Gemfibrozil inhibits CYP2C8 and OATP1B1, dramatically increasing simvastatin levels → myotoxicity. Monitor renal function and electrolytes (hyperkalemia risk from muscle breakdown). Alternative lipid management after recovery: atorvastatin or rosuvastatin (metabolized differently, less interaction risk), ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitor. Fenofibrate (not gemfibrozil) can be used with statins with caution.

77.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with palpitations, irregularly irregular pulse, dizziness, fatigue, and chest discomfort. 80.title: Vomiting
80.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a neonate/infant presenting with bilious (green) vomiting — a surgical emergency until proven otherwise. Bilious vomiting in a newborn = malrotation with volvulus. Malrotation occurs when the midgut fails to complete its normal 270° counterclockwise rotation during fetal development, resulting in a narrow mesenteric base. This predisposes to volvulus — twisting of the midgut around the superior mesenteric artery → intestinal ischemia and necrosis. Diagnosis: upper GI series (gold standard) showing DJJ (duodenojejunal junction) to the RIGHT of midline and spiral/corkscrew duodenum. Abdominal X-ray may show double bubble sign or gasless abdomen. Treatment: EMERGENCY surgical exploration (Ladd procedure). NPO, NG tube decompression, IV fluids. Time-critical — delay leads to bowel necrosis and short gut syndrome.

85.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with oligomenorrhea/amenorrhea, hirsutism, acne, obesity, and infertility. PCOS is the most common endocrine disorder in reproductive-age women. 87.title: Abdominal Pain
87.chiefComplaint: Chronic bloody diarrhea, LLQ pain, tenesmus
87.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with chronic bloody diarrhea, LLQ abdominal cramping, tenesmus, urgency, and weight loss. UC is an inflammatory bowel disease limited to the colon and rectum — inflammation is continuous from the rectum proximally (unlike Crohn's skip lesions), limited to mucosa/submucosa (unlike Crohn's transmural). Extraintestinal manifestations: PSC (most specific), arthritis (axial/peripheral), uveitis, erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum. Diagnosis: colonoscopy with biopsy — continuous inflammation from rectum, friable mucosa, loss of haustra (lead pipe colon on barium enema), crypt abscesses, crypt distortion. Labs: anemia, elevated CRP/ESR, fecal calprotectin, p-ANCA positive. Severity determines treatment: mild → 5-ASA (mesalamine) topical or PO. Moderate → 5-ASA + steroids (prednisone or budesonide MMX). Severe → IV steroids, if refractory → biologics (anti-TNF — infliximab) or JAK inhibitor (tofacitinib). Fulminant/toxic megacolon → cyclosporine or colectomy. Increased colon cancer risk → surveillance colonoscopy starting 8 years after diagnosis.

90.title: Prenatal Followup
90.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a pregnant woman >20 weeks gestation with elevated BP (>140/90 on two occasions at least 4 hours apart) and no proteinuria and no end-organ damage. This is gestational hypertension (PIH) — distinguished from pre-eclampsia by absence of proteinuria and end-organ dysfunction. Risk factors: nulliparity, advanced maternal age, obesity, family history, multiple gestation. Must monitor closely for progression to pre-eclampsia (up to 25% progress). Management: if BP >160/110 → antihypertensive treatment (labetalol, nifedipine ER, methyldopa). If BP 140-159/90-109 → conservative monitoring, no medication needed but close surveillance. If develops pre-eclampsia features → manage as pre-eclampsia. Low-dose aspirin 81mg for pre-eclampsia prevention in high-risk women (started at 12-28 weeks).

Source must be identified: blood cultures x2, urine culture, CXR, and cultures from any suspected site (sputum, wound, CSF). Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 HOUR of recognition — every hour delay increases mortality 7-8%. Initial resuscitation: 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid bolus. Source control: remove lines, drain abscess, debridement if needed.

110.title: Rash
110.chiefComplaint: Diffuse rash involving palms and soles
110.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with rash, lymphadenopathy, and possible genital lesion history. Secondary syphilis: diffuse maculopapular rash (INCLUDING palms and soles — key differentiating feature), condyloma lata (wart-like lesions in moist areas), lymphadenopathy, flu-like symptoms. Follow RPR titers to confirm cure (4-fold decline).

112.title: Found Unconscious
112.chiefComplaint: Found unconscious with signs of physical assault
112.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents found unconscious with signs of physical struggle (bruises, abrasions, torn clothing). Management requires a multidisciplinary, trauma-informed approach. 113.title: Drowning
113.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a child who was submerged in water, presenting with respiratory distress, hypoxia, altered mental status after water rescue. Drowning = respiratory impairment from submersion in liquid. Outcome: death, survival with morbidity, or survival without morbidity. NOT 'near-drowning' in current terminology. Fresh water vs salt water distinction clinically irrelevant — both cause pulmonary surfactant washout → ARDS. Key: hypoxic brain injury determines prognosis. 118.title: Muscle Pain
118.chiefComplaint: Diffuse muscle pain, dark urine, weakness
118.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with diffuse muscle pain, weakness, dark cola-colored urine (myoglobinuria), and fatigue following prolonged immobilization, crush injury, extreme exertion, or medication reaction. Labs: markedly elevated CK (often >5,000, can be >100,000), elevated Cr (AKI from myoglobin), hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia. UA positive for blood on dipstick but no RBCs on microscopy (myoglobinuria). Rhabdomyolysis = skeletal muscle breakdown → release of intracellular contents (K, phosphate, myoglobin, CK) into bloodstream. Biggest risk: acute kidney injury from myoglobin pigment nephropathy. Management: AGGRESSIVE IV crystalloid resuscitation (NS or LR, 1-2L bolus then 200-300 mL/hr titrated to urine output >200-300 mL/hr). Monitor urine output, renal function, electrolytes (hyperkalemia → cardiac arrhythmia). Alkalinization with bicarb generally NOT recommended. Treat underlying cause.

123.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with unilateral leg swelling, pain, warmth, and erythema. Risk factors: Virchow's triad — stasis (immobilization, long travel), hypercoagulability (malignancy, OCPs, pregnancy, thrombophilia), endothelial injury (surgery, trauma). Exam: Homan's sign unreliable. Measure leg circumference difference. Wells criteria determines pretest probability. If low probability → D-dimer. If D-dimer elevated or high probability → compression ultrasound (proximal DVT). Treatment: most DVT → anticoagulation with DOAC (rivaroxaban, apixaban) or LMWH bridge to warfarin. Duration: provoked = 3 months, unprovoked = 6-12 months or indefinite. NO routine thrombectomy or IVC filter unless anticoagulation contraindicated. Compression stockings for symptom relief and post-thrombotic syndrome prevention.

125.title: Chest Pain
125.chiefComplaint: Chest pain, hypotension, clear lungs, elevated JVP
125.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with chest pain, hypotension, clear lung fields, elevated JVP, and Kussmaul's sign. ECG shows ST elevation in inferior leads (II, III, aVF) with ST elevation in V1 > V3 and ST elevation in V4R (right-sided leads) — indicating RV involvement. RV infarction occurs in ~30% of inferior MIs (usually RCA occlusion). RV is preload-dependent — nitroglycerin and morphine can cause dangerous hypotension because they reduce preload. Treatment: AVOID nitrates and diuretics (reduce preload → worsen RV output). Give IV fluids aggressively to maintain RV preload. Aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitor, anticoagulation. REPERFUSION: emergent PCI (preferred) or fibrinolysis. If hypotensive despite fluids: dobutamine (inotrope). Atropine for bradycardia. Admit to CCU.

127.title: Rash
127.chiefComplaint: Petechiae, purpura, easy bruising in well child
127.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with sudden onset petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gum bleeding, and possibly mucosal bleeding in an otherwise well-appearing child. No lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no fever, no bone pain — distinguishes from leukemia. ITP is an autoimmune destruction of platelets (antibodies against GPIIb/IIIa). Often preceded by viral URI or vaccination 1-4 weeks prior. Labs: ISOLATED thrombocytopenia (platelets <100K, often <20K). Normal Hb, normal WBC, normal peripheral smear (except low platelets). Bone marrow biopsy NOT needed in typical childhood ITP. Treatment: most children (>80%) recover spontaneously within 6 months. If platelets >20K and no bleeding → observation only. If <10K or significant bleeding → prednisone 2-4 mg/kg/day or IVIG or anti-D (if Rh+). Avoid IM injections, contact sports, NSAIDs/aspirin.

130.title: Cough
130.chiefComplaint: High fever, cough, GI symptoms, hyponatremia
130.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with high fever, cough (initially dry then productive), dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and extrapulmonary symptoms: GI (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain), hyponatremia (classic lab finding), confusion/AMS, relative bradycardia. History: exposure to contaminated water sources (hot tubs, cooling towers, hotel, cruise ship). Legionella is an atypical pneumonia — intracellular pathogen not seen on Gram stain. Diagnosis: urinary antigen test (detects L. pneumophila serogroup 1 — most common, rapid), sputum culture on specialized media (BCYE agar), PCR. Severe cases require hospitalization. Treatment: macrolides (azithromycin) or respiratory fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin). Doxycycline as alternative. Treatment duration 7-14 days (longer if immunocompromised). Report to public health (Legionnaires disease is reportable).

133.title: Back Pain
133.chiefComplaint: Chronic low back pain, morning stiffness improved by exercise
133.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with chronic low back pain (>3 months), morning stiffness (>30 min) that IMPROVES with exercise and WORSENS with rest. Inflammatory back pain pattern (vs mechanical — worsens with activity). Associated: sacroiliitis, limited spinal mobility (Schober test), enthesitis, peripheral arthritis, uveitis. Young male predominance. Strong association with HLA-B27. Diagnosis: X-ray/MRI of SI joints — sacroiliitis (bamboo spine in advanced disease). Elevated ESR/CRP. Treatment: NSAIDs first-line (excellent response — diagnostic feature). Physical therapy — maintain posture and mobility. If NSAIDs insufficient → TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept). IL-17 inhibitors (secukinumab) also effective. Do NOT recommend bed rest — makes it worse. Exercise program essential.

135.title: Muscle Weakness
135.diagnosis: Hyperkalemic Emergency secondary to ACE Inhibitor + NSAID
135.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with progressive muscle weakness, fatigue, and palpitations. ECG shows peaked T waves, loss of P waves, widened QRS. Labs reveal severe hyperkalemia (K+ >6.5). Medication history: on ACE inhibitor for HTN and recently started NSAIDs for joint pain. ACEI reduces aldosterone → decreased renal K+ excretion. NSAIDs reduce renal blood flow → further decrease K+ excretion. Combined → dangerous hyperkalemia. Management: IMMEDIATE cardiac membrane stabilization — IV calcium gluconate or calcium chloride (does NOT lower K+, PROTECTS the heart). Then shift K+ intracellularly: IV regular insulin + glucose, beta-agonist (albuterol nebulized), sodium bicarbonate if acidotic. Then eliminate K+: furosemide (if renal function adequate), sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate), patiromer, or hemodialysis if refractory. Discontinue ACEI and NSAIDs.

136.title: Shortness of Breath
136.chiefComplaint: Progressive dyspnea, dry cough, bilateral hilar adenopathy
136.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with progressive dyspnea, dry cough, fatigue, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on CXR. May have erythema nodosum (painful red nodules on shins), uveitis, parotid enlargement, lupus pernio (purplish facial plaques). Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disease of unknown etiology — more common in African Americans. Non-caseating granulomas are the pathologic hallmark. CXR staging: I (BHL only), II (BHL + parenchymal infiltrates), III (parenchymal only), IV (fibrosis). Labs: elevated ACE level (supports but not diagnostic), hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria (increased 1,25-vitamin D from activated macrophages in granulomas). Diagnosis: biopsy showing non-caseating granulomas + exclusion of other causes (TB, fungal, berylliosis). PFTs: restrictive pattern. Treatment: many resolve spontaneously (stage I). If symptomatic or progressive → corticosteroids (prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/day). Methotrexate or azathioprine for steroid-sparing. Anti-TNF for refractory. Monitor for TB reactivation before immunosuppression.

138.title: Fatigue
138.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with progressive fatigue, weakness, anorexia, nausea, pruritus, edema, and oliguria. Labs: markedly elevated BUN/Cr, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, anemia (low EPO), hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism. ESRD is irreversible loss of renal function (GFR <15). Most common causes: diabetes, hypertension, glomerulonephritis. Management: renal replacement therapy — hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, or kidney transplant. Urgent indications for dialysis: AEIOU — Acidosis, Electrolytes (hyperkalemia), Intoxication (toxins), Overload (volume), Uremia (pericarditis, encephalopathy). 146.title: Found Unconscious

146.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents found unconscious with cherry-red skin, bitter almond breath odor (only 40% can detect), high anion gap metabolic acidosis, and elevated lactate. 148.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with pleuritic chest pain, fever, malaise, and pericardial friction rub 2-6 weeks after a myocardial infarction. Dressler syndrome is an autoimmune-mediated pericarditis occurring post-MI (or post-cardiac surgery) — immune response to exposed myocardial antigens. ECG: diffuse ST elevation, PR depression (pericarditis pattern). Echo: pericardial effusion (usually small). 156.title: Generalized Swelling
156.chiefComplaint: Generalized edema, frothy urine, weight gain
156.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} is a child presenting with generalized edema (periorbital — worse in morning, then leg/scrotal), weight gain, frothy urine (proteinuria), and fatigue. Nephrotic syndrome: massive proteinuria (>3.5g/day or >40mg/m2/hr in children), hypoalbuminemia (<2.5), edema, hyperlipidemia. Most common cause in children: minimal change disease (MCD) — 80-90%. Diuretics for severe edema. If steroid-resistant or frequently relapsing: consider biopsy, alternative immunosuppression (cyclophosphamide, cyclosporine). Vaccinate before immunosuppression (pneumococcal). Monitor for complications: infection (loss of immunoglobulins), thrombosis (loss of antithrombin III).

173.title: Sexual Assault
173.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents after sexual assault. Management: trauma-informed, multidisciplinary approach. Medical stabilization first, then forensic examination with consent. SANE examination if available. Forensic evidence collection (rape kit) within 72h. Document injuries. Labs: STI testing (CT, GC, HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B/C), toxicology if concern for drug-facilitated assault. Empiric STI prophylaxis: ceftriaxone + doxycycline + metronidazole. HIV PEP if exposure within 72h (28-day course). Hepatitis B vaccine if not immune. Mental health crisis counseling. Report to law enforcement (with patient consent). Safe discharge planning. Follow-up: STI re-testing, counseling.

181.title: Nocturnal Enuresis
181.diagnosis: Severe Obstructive Sleep Apnea with Secondary Nocturnal Enuresis
181.chiefComplaint: Nocturnal enuresis, loud snoring, daytime fatigue
181.hpiNarrative: {{patient_name}} presents with primary or secondary nocturnal enuresis (bedwetting), loud snoring, restless sleep, daytime fatigue, and behavioral issues. Severe OSA causes nocturnal enuresis through: (1) increased intra-abdominal pressure during apnea → increased venous return → ANP/BNP release → increased nocturnal urine production; (2) disrupted sleep architecture → decreased arousal to bladder distention. Polysomnography confirms severe OSA (AHI >30). Treatment: CPAP or adenotonsillectomy if large tonsils/adenoids. Treating the OSA often resolves the enuresis. Do NOT treat enuresis in isolation without evaluating for sleep-disordered breathing.
